I released z386, an open-source 80386 CPU core, in May and added the 80386 early-start optimization in June. Early start overlaps address generation for one instruction with completion of its predecessor. It was an important 386 performance feature, but it also previewed the more systematic i486 pipeline. The MiSTer core needed more performance, so I continued in that direction and added further 486-class mechanisms.

The result is z486, an open-source, 80486-class pipelined x86 CPU written in SystemVerilog. It combines hardwired, pipelined execution for common instructions with microcode for complex architectural behavior.

z486 is not an i486 clone. Its design draws on three i486-inspired elements:

  1. a pipelined D1/D2 frontend;
  2. hardwired execution of common instructions, with microcode retained for complex instructions; and
  3. an experimental integrated x87 unit implementing the subset exercised by Quake.

On the same MiSTer system, the current core runs the Doom timedemo at 29.1 FPS at maximum detail, compared with 21.0 FPS on ao486. This is roughly 486DX2-66-class performance for the measured workload. Dhrystone reaches 0.330 DMIPS/MHz, versus 0.225 for z386 and 0.194 for ao486. These results show that a practical pipelined x86 CPU with broad architectural support, including x87, can fit on a mid-range FPGA.

The i486 five-stage pipeline

A finite-state or microcoded CPU limits combinational depth by performing decode, address generation, memory access, ALU work, and commit in separate cycles. This supports a high clock frequency but gives simple instructions a high cycles-per-instruction (CPI) count. Combining all work into one cycle reduces CPI but creates long paths through wide multiplexers and interconnect. Pipelining separates the work with registers and overlaps successive instructions.

Variable-length x86 instructions require a different stage division from the classic RISC pipeline, commonly written as IF-ID-EX-MEM-WB. The i486 uses five stages:

Stage Main work
FI Fetch a 16-byte line into the instruction queue.
D1 Decode prefixes, opcode, ModR/M structure, instruction length, and D2 actions.
D2 Capture displacement or immediate data and calculate an effective address.
EX Execute ALU or microcode work; access cache and TLB for memory instructions.
WB Write an ALU or load result into the register file.

The two decode stages replace the single RISC ID stage, and cache access occurs in EX rather than in a separate MEM stage. Microcoded instructions can use several EX cycles. One-clock throughput is therefore the common case, not a property of every instruction.

Intel's functional block diagram, reproduced with the references, shows how internal buses connect decode, address generation, translation, cache access, and execution.

Decoding variable-length x86 instructions

By the time the i486 was designed, x86 instructions already had a complex, variable-length encoding. Prefixes, two-byte opcodes, ModR/M and SIB bytes, displacements, and immediates are all optional, and some fields cannot be located until earlier fields have been interpreted. Earlier x86 frontends used sequential decode machinery that could take several clocks. The i486 instead divides decode into two explicit pipeline stages: D1 determines instruction structure and boundaries, while D2 captures literals and generates addresses.

In the common case, D1 decodes the opcode, ModR/M, and SIB together. It also determines the instruction length and tells the aligner where both the next instruction and the current instruction's literals begin. Prefixes are processed one byte per clock, and a 0F escape consumes another D1 clock.

D2 consumes one 1- to 4-byte displacement or immediate per clock. In parallel, it reads the base and index registers and calculates the effective address. Separate structural and literal ports in the prefetch queue let D1 work on one instruction while D2 works on its predecessor.

Common forms complete D2 in one clock. Two cases extend D2:

  • an instruction with both a displacement and an immediate uses two D2 clocks;
  • an address containing base, displacement, and scaled index can use a second D2 clock for the second addition.

This is also the pipelined version of the 386's early-start idea. On the 386, the instruction queue presents address operands during the final cycle of the previous instruction. On the i486, D2 is an explicit stage where the next instruction performs the same work while its predecessors occupy EX and WB.

The extra cycles are a deliberate area and timing tradeoff. Allowing both decoders to select every field from every possible byte position in the prefetch queue would require large alignment networks. The bounded D1 and D2 windows keep common instructions fast without making worst-case alignment part of the clock-critical datapath.

Loads, forwarding, and the pointer-load delay

Overlapping instructions introduce data hazards when a successor needs a result that its predecessor has not yet written to the register file. Consider a load followed immediately by an ALU operation:

mov eax, [esi]
add ebx, eax

When ADD reaches EX, the load result is in WB but may not yet be visible through a normal register-file read. Stalling until the write completes would create a data-load delay.

On the i486, given a cache hit, forwarding makes the value available to an ordinary dependent ALU instruction in the same cycle. Consequently, the i486 has no general data-load delay.

The exception is a successor that uses the loaded register as an address base or index:

mov eax, [esi]
mov ebx, [eax]

The second MOV needs EAX in D2 to calculate the effective address that its memory access will use in EX. This is one stage earlier than an ALU consumer needs the value. When the second instruction first reaches D2, the load is still in EX and its result is unavailable. D2 must stall for one clock, then receive the value when the load advances to WB. Intel called this the pointer-load delay; today it is commonly described as an address-generation interlock, or AGI.

Eliminating this delay would require an earlier and larger bypass network. The i486 instead accepts a one-cycle bubble for pointer dependencies.

Branch timing

The i486 evaluates a conditional branch in EX while speculatively fetching the target. A not-taken Jcc costs one clock because the sequential pipeline is already present. A taken Jcc, JMP, or near CALL takes three clocks from branch EX to target EX.

Crawford reports that Intel evaluated a more aggressive two-cycle taken-branch design, but it would have made not-taken branches slower and required significantly more cache machinery. The published instruction mix showed only about a one-percent overall advantage. The implemented three-cycle-taken, one-cycle-not-taken policy fit the rest of the pipeline better.

The z486 pipeline

Using the i486 pipeline as a guide, z486 retains its FI, D1, D2, and EX stage division. The main difference is at the back end: ordinary integer results commit on the EX edge rather than passing through a general WB stage.

The implementation maps this stage flow onto hardwired and microcoded control paths that share the same address, data, memory, protection, and floating-point units. The RTL is also more modular than z386. Address generation, integer execution, memory, hardwired control, and microsequencing were extracted into separate modules, leaving z486.sv primarily as pipeline integration and cross-unit glue. The resulting top-level module is about one-third shorter than z386's: 2.6K lines versus 3.9K.

The frontend uses a 32-byte prefetch queue filled one 16-byte instruction-cache line at a time. Like the i486 queue, it provides separate ports for structural and literal decode: a registered 64-bit D1 window and a 32-bit literal window. Prefixes and 0F consume extra structural cycles. An opcode and optional ModR/M normally complete in one D1 clock, while SIB parsing can use a retained sub-cycle. A one-entry registered skid buffer lets D1 run ahead when D2 is occupied without requiring a deep decoded-instruction queue.

D1 resolves the microcode entry and launches it into the synchronous control store. The first control word is therefore available in D2 alongside the decoded instruction and its literals. D2 performs effective-address work and hazard checks; i_issue is the single event that transfers the completed D2 instruction into EX.

This organization keeps two expensive operations out of the same cycle:

  • D2 calculates and relocates the effective address to a linear address;
  • the next part of the memory path translates it and accesses the physically indexed, physically tagged cache.

The release MiSTer configuration has separate 8 KB instruction and 8 KB data caches, both four-way set associative with 16-byte lines. The data cache is write-through with a three-entry store queue. The i486 instead has one unified 8 KB cache and completes a cache-hit load in one clock by overlapping virtual indexing with translation. z486 has twice the total L1 capacity, but its simpler physically indexed, physically tagged organization serializes translation and cache access. A best-case integer load therefore takes two clocks rather than the i486's one. Getting VIPT to work is future work.

Write-back organization

z486 differs from the i486 at the back end. Ordinary GPR, EIP, ESP, EFLAGS, and internal-register results commit on the EX clock edge; there is no general WB stage.

This is an FPGA-specific tradeoff. Preserving dependency timing with a full WB stage requires a broad bypass network: younger instructions need pending WB values in EX and, for address dependencies, one stage earlier in D2. In earlier experiments, the additional routing and operand-mux delay cost more than moving commit out of the EX critical paths saved. z486 therefore retains only narrow, operation-specific deferred state, such as a shifter result or a pending load commit.

Hardwiring common instructions

Pipelining does not automatically remove the original 386 microcode's two-cycle minimum for simple operations. Register MOV, for example, is:

003  SRCREG                           PASS    RNI
004  SIGMA  -> DSTREG

The first word passes the source through the ALU and announces run-next-instruction (RNI). Because the sequencer has an architectural delay slot, the second word still executes and writes the result. Running this sequence unchanged would retain a two-cycle EX retirement rate despite the faster frontend.

The i486 controls frequent instructions with hardwired logic while retaining microcode for complex cases. z486 follows the same division: hardwired and microcoded control both drive the shared integer datapath.

Recipes and uSteps

The generation script scripts/ucode_optimize.py produces metadata for 34 hardwired instruction recipes. Each recipe contains one to three active uSteps. A uStep combines a native microcode word with generated fields for D2 work, architectural commit, delay-slot handling, and hazards.

For MOV r,r, the optimized word still uses the original PASS datapath, but a generated destination encoding commits the ALU result on the same edge. The hardwired recipe therefore completes the same work in one active slot.

Chaining

Once a delay slot is proven redundant, z486 may start the next hardwired instruction in it. This is called chaining. It applies to both one- and multi-uStep recipes: a one-uStep recipe can launch its registered successor at issue, while a multi-uStep recipe can launch the queue head when its final RNI word is approaching. Repeated one-uStep chains provide sustained one-instruction-per-clock execution.

Before chaining, the control unit checks:

  • source, destination, and byte-register overlap;
  • flags producer/consumer dependencies;
  • effective-address base, index, and ESP dependencies;
  • pending load and shift destinations;
  • D2 and control-store residency;
  • whether a memory or stack slot still contains real work; and
  • faults, interrupts, traps, single-step, and CPU throttling.

Memory, stack, and branches

Recipes are not limited to register operations:

  • MOV r,[m] prepares the address in D2 and uses a two-uStep load recipe, retaining a real result slot;
  • stores and PUSH keep their memory slot because acceptance and ESP update are architectural work;
  • safe not-taken Jcc can fold into the predecessor boundary;
  • taken Jcc and JMP use the D2-computed relative target in one bounded branch uStep; and
  • near CALL combines redirect, posted return-address store, and ESP commit.

The current best-case instruction timing is:

Instruction class 80386 i486 z486
MOV r,r / ADD r,r 2 1 1
MOV r,[m] 4 1 2
MOV [m],r 2 1 1
ADD r,[m] 5 2 3
Jcc not taken 3 1 1
Jcc taken about 9 3 3
JMP taken about 9 3 3
near CALL about 9 3 4
XCHG [m],r 5 5 5

The main remaining gap is memory latency: z486's PIPT data cache takes two clocks for a load hit. A timing-safe VIPT design is one possible route to the i486's one-clock load.

Instructions without a hardwired recipe continue through the general microsequencer. Task switching, call gates, privilege transitions, descriptor updates, nested faults, unusual prefixes, and other complex behavior therefore retain the original microcode routines and their delay-slot assumptions.

z486 includes an experimental integrated x87 floating-point unit. It is not yet a complete x87 implementation, but it implements enough of the instruction set to run Quake and TurboQuake. Its organization follows the major boundaries of the original 80387, whose block diagram appears in the references: command and stack control, a microcoded numeric executor, shared significand arithmetic, and a separate CORDIC engine for transcendental functions.

  • x87_bridge converts the 80386 command/data-port protocol into registered ready/valid transfers;
  • x87_control owns command decode, the stack, TOP, tags, status, exceptions, and architectural commit;
  • x87_executor runs a generated 256-word horizontal control store over shared conversion and arithmetic resources; and
  • a qualified direct-m32 overlay removes the long 386 command/data transfer loop from common game instructions while preserving normal paging and fault checks.

The integer-only z386 core already occupied about 15,000 ALMs, while a complete PC configuration with caches, memory control, and peripherals exceeded 25,000. The Cyclone V on the DE10-Nano provides 41,910 ALMs, so a conventional FPU could easily exhaust the remaining capacity or make the design impractical to place and route. Three implementation choices keep the unit within this limited area budget:

  1. Horizontal microcode and shared arithmetic. A synchronous 256-word by 64-bit control store sequences the numeric executor. Each horizontal word independently controls flow, operand preparation, classification, the add/subtract and shift routes, iterative engines, rounding state, result packing, commit, and CORDIC scratch accesses. This replaces a large decoded operation selector with direct control of the state updated by each step. Addition, normalization, conversion, and rounding share a 68-bit work register and adder. Division and square root reuse iterative datapaths, while the infrequent transcendental instructions use a microcoded, limb-oriented CORDIC engine.

  2. Reduced internal precision. The architectural stack and transfer paths retain raw 80-bit temporary-real values, preserving untouched FLD m80 to FSTP m80 round trips and save/restore data. Arithmetic decodes an operand into a 15-bit exponent and a 53-bit significand, with separate guard, round, and sticky state. The add/subtract path carries those 53 retained bits plus overflow and rounding positions in a 57-bit active slice of the shared work register. This keeps the 80387 exponent range but provides binary64-class precision rather than the 80387's full 64-bit significand. Results produced by arithmetic therefore have reduced precision even when stored as m80.

  3. DSP-based multiplication. The two 53-bit significands are split into 27- and 26-bit limbs. Four 27-by-27 products map onto Cyclone V DSP blocks and are assembled into an exact 106-bit intermediate product. This avoids a large LUT multiplier while retaining all bits needed by the common rounder.

With these measures, the FPU hierarchy uses about 5,100 ALMs in the 85 MHz release fit. The complete z486 PC build, including the FPU and peripherals, uses 35,686 of the DE10-Nano's 41,910 ALMs.

Performance was optimized iteratively as well. In an early TurboQuake render-window profile, x87 instructions accounted for about 23% of retired instructions but 61% of instruction-attributed cycles. The numeric executor was active during only about 40% of those x87 cycles; command dispatch, operand transfer, stack access, launch, and retirement consumed the rest. Performance work therefore addressed both sides of the CPU/FPU boundary: faster conversion and arithmetic schedules, a direct m32 path for common memory operands, and shorter command sequencing.

The first complete x87 build ran TurboQuake at 2.7 FPS at 50 MHz. The current release reaches about 6.3 FPS at the 85 MHz board clock.

Performance evaluation

Dhrystone: CPU performance

Dhrystone provides a compact measure of integer pipeline efficiency, largely separate from clock rate and whole-system behavior. The evaluation covers z386, ao486, z486, PicoRV32, and VexRiscv.

The benchmark uses the conventional VAX 11/780 normalization:

DMIPS/MHz = iterations * 1,000,000 / (cycles * 1757)

All builds use -O3 -fno-inline, no link-time optimization, and no explicit register declarations. The x86 cores execute the same i386 binary produced by GCC 11.4. PicoRV32 and VexRiscv execute the same C source as RV32IM, built by GCC 10.2. Each harness returns memory data at the earliest cycle allowed by its interface. z386 and z486 retain the release 8 KB instruction and 8 KB data caches; ao486 retains its native cache organization.

Core Cycles/iteration CPI DMIPS/MHz Cyclone V ALMs
z386 2,526.4 4.101 0.225 15,545
ao486 2,934.0 4.556 0.194 15,190
z486 1,725.0 2.800 0.330 21,906
PicoRV32 2,336.1 4.172 0.244 1,202
VexRiscv 780.1 1.393 0.730 1,029

The ALM figures come from standalone seed-1 fits on the DE10-Nano Cyclone V, all using the same z486_MiSTer production settings. The configurations are not feature-equivalent: the two RISC-V cores omit caches, an MMU, segmentation, protected mode, legacy I/O and interrupts, and floating point. A z486 build without x87 uses 16,329 ALMs, only 5.0% more than z386.

z486 uses 31.7% fewer cycles per iteration than z386 and 41.2% fewer than ao486. Its DMIPS/MHz is 46% above z386 and 70% above ao486. At the tested MiSTer clocks, the results are 28.05 DMIPS for z486 at 85 MHz, 19.15 for z386 at 85 MHz, and 17.46 for ao486 at 90 MHz. Source repositories, release clocks, and upstream results are listed in Further information and references.

Compiler and memory-interface choices have a large effect on Dhrystone scores. The local no-cache VexRiscv RV32IM build reaches 0.730 DMIPS/MHz, below the project's published 1.21 DMIPS/MHz for its full no-cache configuration and documented benchmark environment. PicoRV32 reaches 0.244 DMIPS/MHz locally; its project reports 0.516 with the look-ahead memory interface and 0.305 without it. The published configurations are linked in the final reference section.

CPI is derived from each binary's retired instruction count, so it should be compared across ISAs less precisely than cycles per iteration or DMIPS/MHz. The ao486 retirement event also occurs at a different pipeline boundary from the z386 and z486 event. These differences do not affect the measured cycle counts.

Doom: whole-system performance

Doom measures whole-system performance rather than isolated integer pipeline efficiency. Its timedemo exercises instruction decode and execution, caches, external memory, and video writes. All measurements use the same MiSTer setup at each core's release clock: 85 MHz for z386 and z486, and 90 MHz for ao486.

At maximum detail, z486 reaches 29.1 FPS in the Doom timedemo, 39% faster than ao486's 21.0 FPS and 27% faster than z386 v0.4's 23.0 FPS. The independent 3DBench result shows the same ordering. Doom represents complete DOS-system behavior; Dhrystone more directly isolates integer pipeline efficiency.

Verification

Verification for a pipelining CPU is harder than a sequential one as there is more parallelism. A value may belong to the wrong instruction, a fault may cancel EX while leaving a younger commit active, or a cache operation may race with a store or DMA snoop. Validation therefore covers both instruction semantics and inter-stage ordering.

The current validation stack includes:

  • directed single-instruction tests;
  • 9,410 real-mode and 1,220 protected-mode singlestep cases;
  • protected-mode integration programs and the test386 suite;
  • focused instruction/data cache race tests;
  • x87 command, stack, executor, TestFloat, and CPU integration tests;
  • differential x87 traces against QEMU and a retired reference executor;
  • deterministic Doom and Quake snapshots with RAM hashes;
  • full-system DOS, Windows 3.1, Doom, Quake, demos, and game simulations; and
  • five-seed Quartus comparisons followed by physical MiSTer testing.

ao486 is the closest related open-source design and the CPU behind the established ao486 MiSTer core. It implements a 486SX-class integer processor with broad software compatibility, but no integrated x87. ao486 implements the 486 architecture directly; z486 instead evolved from a microcoded 386 core, adding a pipelined frontend, generated hardwired recipes for common instructions, and an application-focused x87. Because both run the same PC software on the same FPGA platform, their whole-system Doom results are more informative than area alone.

Open RISC-V cores cover a larger design space, from multi-cycle PicoRV32 to configurable pipelined VexRiscv. They provide useful Dhrystone and FPGA-efficiency reference points, but are not area-equivalent alternatives: the x86 cores also implement variable-length decode, segmented and paged protection, legacy execution modes, and a much larger compatibility surface.

Potential work includes:

  • improving sustained cache-hit load throughput;
  • reclaiming more redundant instruction-boundary slots through measured, timing-safe chaining;
  • completing the remaining 486 and x87 instructions;
  • moving x87 arithmetic toward the full 64-bit significand of the 80387;
  • improving 85 MHz timing margin while retaining current CPI and area; and
  • continuing compatibility work driven by DOS and Windows games and applications.

Conclusion

z486 shows that a microcode-driven 386 foundation can be extended into a practical pipelined FPGA CPU without replacing its complex architectural behavior with a large behavioral instruction engine. The D1/D2 frontend and generated hardwired recipes give common instructions i486-like timing, while the original microcode continues to handle protection, faults, task switching, and other irregular operations. A compact integrated x87 extends that approach to the floating-point subset needed by Quake.

The resulting core reaches 0.330 DMIPS/MHz and runs the maximum-detail Doom timedemo at 29.1 FPS on MiSTer, compared with 0.194 DMIPS/MHz and 21.0 FPS for ao486. It does so at 85 MHz in 35,686 of the DE10-Nano's 41,910 ALMs. The remaining two-cycle load latency, incomplete x87 instruction set, and limited timing margin also show where the FPGA implementation still differs from a complete i486-class processor.

Further information and references

These notes collect the diagrams, historical sources, reverse-engineering work, benchmark configurations, and implementations discussed in this article.

That organization is the main architectural reference for z486's integer pipeline.

Branch timing The i486 evaluates a conditional branch in EX while speculatively fetching the target. A not-taken Jcc costs one clock because the sequential pipeline is already present. A taken Jcc, JMP, or near CALL takes three clocks from branch EX to target EX. Branch EX evaluates the condition and starts target FI. The sequential path reaches EX after one clock; the taken target reaches EX after three. Redrawn from Crawford, reference 3, Figure 6. Crawford reports that Intel evaluated a more aggressive two-cycle taken-branch design, but it would have made not-taken branches slower and required significantly more cache machinery. The published instruction mix showed only about a one-percent overall advantage. The implemented three-cycle-taken, one-cycle-not-taken policy fit the rest of the pipeline better. The z486 pipeline Using the i486 pipeline as a guide, z486 retains its FI, D1, D2, and EX stage division. The main difference is at the back end: ordinary integer results commit on the EX edge rather than passing through a general WB stage. z486 follows the i486 frontend organization but combines ordinary integer execution and commit. The implementation maps this stage flow onto hardwired and microcoded control paths that share the same address, data, memory, protection, and floating-point units. The RTL is also more modular than z386. Address generation, integer execution, memory, hardwired control, and microsequencing were extracted into separate modules, leaving z486.sv primarily as pipeline integration and cross-unit glue. The resulting top-level module is about one-third shorter than z386's: 2.6K lines versus 3.9K. The implemented z486 organization. Hardwired and microcoded instructions share the same datapath. The frontend uses a 32-byte prefetch queue filled one 16-byte instruction-cache line at a time. Like the i486 queue, it provides separate ports for structural and literal decode: a registered 64-bit D1 window and a 32-bit literal window. Prefixes and 0F consume extra structural cycles. An opcode and optional ModR/M normally complete in one D1 clock, while SIB parsing can use a retained sub-cycle. A one-entry registered skid buffer lets D1 run ahead when D2 is occupied without requiring a deep decoded-instruction queue. D1 resolves the microcode entry and launches it into the synchronous control store. The first control word is therefore available in D2 alongside the decoded instruction and its literals. D2 performs effective-address work and hazard checks; i_issue is the single event that transfers the completed D2 instruction into EX. This organization keeps two expensive operations out of the same cycle: D2 calculates and relocates the effective address to a linear address; the next part of the memory path translates it and accesses the physically indexed, physically tagged cache. The release MiSTer configuration has separate 8 KB instruction and 8 KB data caches, both four-way set associative with 16-byte lines. The data cache is write-through with a three-entry store queue. The i486 instead has one unified 8 KB cache and completes a cache-hit load in one clock by overlapping virtual indexing with translation. z486 has twice the total L1 capacity, but its simpler physically indexed, physically tagged organization serializes translation and cache access. A best-case integer load therefore takes two clocks rather than the i486's one. Getting VIPT to work is future work. Write-back organization z486 differs from the i486 at the back end. Ordinary GPR, EIP, ESP, EFLAGS, and internal-register results commit on the EX clock edge; there is no general WB stage. This is an FPGA-specific tradeoff. Preserving dependency timing with a full WB stage requires a broad bypass network: younger instructions need pending WB values in EX and, for address dependencies, one stage earlier in D2. In earlier experiments, the additional routing and operand-mux delay cost more than moving commit out of the EX critical paths saved. z486 therefore retains only narrow, operation-specific deferred state, such as a shifter result or a pending load commit. Hardwiring common instructions Pipelining does not automatically remove the original 386 microcode's two-cycle minimum for simple operations. Register MOV, for example, is: 003 SRCREG PASS RNI 004 SIGMA -> DSTREG The first word passes the source through the ALU and announces run-next-instruction (RNI). Because the sequencer has an architectural delay slot, the second word still executes and writes the result. Running this sequence unchanged would retain a two-cycle EX retirement rate despite the faster frontend. The i486 controls frequent instructions with hardwired logic while retaining microcode for complex cases. z486 follows the same division: hardwired and microcoded control both drive the shared integer datapath. Recipes and uSteps The generation script scripts/ucode_optimize.py produces metadata for 34 hardwired instruction recipes. Each recipe contains one to three active uSteps. A uStep combines a native microcode word with generated fields for D2 work, architectural commit, delay-slot handling, and hazards. For MOV r,r, the optimized word still uses the original PASS datapath, but a generated destination encoding commits the ALU result on the same edge. The hardwired recipe therefore completes the same work in one active slot. A recipe folds the delay-slot effect into the RNI word, reclaiming one execution slot. Chaining Once a delay slot is proven redundant, z486 may start the next hardwired instruction in it. This is called chaining. It applies to both one- and multi-uStep recipes: a one-uStep recipe can launch its registered successor at issue, while a multi-uStep recipe can launch the queue head when its final RNI word is approaching. Repeated one-uStep chains provide sustained one-instruction-per-clock execution. Before chaining, the control unit checks: source, destination, and byte-register overlap; flags producer/consumer dependencies; effective-address base, index, and ESP dependencies; pending load and shift destinations; D2 and control-store residency; whether a memory or stack slot still contains real work; and faults, interrupts, traps, single-step, and CPU throttling. Memory, stack, and branches Recipes are not limited to register operations: MOV r,[m] prepares the address in D2 and uses a two-uStep load recipe, retaining a real result slot; stores and PUSH keep their memory slot because acceptance and ESP update are architectural work; safe not-taken Jcc can fold into the predecessor boundary; taken Jcc and JMP use the D2-computed relative target in one bounded branch uStep; and near CALL combines redirect, posted return-address store, and ESP commit. The current best-case instruction timing is: Instruction class 80386 i486 z486 MOV r,r / ADD r,r 2 1 1 MOV r,[m] 4 1 2 MOV [m],r 2 1 1 ADD r,[m] 5 2 3 Jcc not taken 3 1 1 Jcc taken about 9 3 3 JMP taken about 9 3 3 near CALL about 9 3 4 XCHG [m],r 5 5 5 The main remaining gap is memory latency: z486's PIPT data cache takes two clocks for a load hit. A timing-safe VIPT design is one possible route to the i486's one-clock load. Instructions without a hardwired recipe continue through the general microsequencer. Task switching, call gates, privilege transitions, descriptor updates, nested faults, unusual prefixes, and other complex behavior therefore retain the original microcode routines and their delay-slot assumptions. z486 includes an experimental integrated x87 floating-point unit. It is not yet a complete x87 implementation, but it implements enough of the instruction set to run Quake and TurboQuake. Its organization follows the major boundaries of the original 80387, whose block diagram appears in the references: command and stack control, a microcoded numeric executor, shared significand arithmetic, and a separate CORDIC engine for transcendental functions. x87_bridge converts the 80386 command/data-port protocol into registered ready/valid transfers; x87_control owns command decode, the stack, TOP, tags, status, exceptions, and architectural commit; x87_executor runs a generated 256-word horizontal control store over shared conversion and arithmetic resources; and a qualified direct-m32 overlay removes the long 386 command/data transfer loop from common game instructions while preserving normal paging and fault checks. The current z486 x87. It follows the 80387's control/FPU division, but uses FPGA block RAMs and DSPs. The integer-only z386 core already occupied about 15,000 ALMs, while a complete PC configuration with caches, memory control, and peripherals exceeded 25,000. The Cyclone V on the DE10-Nano provides 41,910 ALMs, so a conventional FPU could easily exhaust the remaining capacity or make the design impractical to place and route. Three implementation choices keep the unit within this limited area budget: Horizontal microcode and shared arithmetic. A synchronous 256-word by 64-bit control store sequences the numeric executor. Each horizontal word independently controls flow, operand preparation, classification, the add/subtract and shift routes, iterative engines, rounding state, result packing, commit, and CORDIC scratch accesses. This replaces a large decoded operation selector with direct control of the state updated by each step. Addition, normalization, conversion, and rounding share a 68-bit work register and adder. Division and square root reuse iterative datapaths, while the infrequent transcendental instructions use a microcoded, limb-oriented CORDIC engine. Reduced internal precision. The architectural stack and transfer paths retain raw 80-bit temporary-real values, preserving untouched FLD m80 to FSTP m80 round trips and save/restore data. Arithmetic decodes an operand into a 15-bit exponent and a 53-bit significand, with separate guard, round, and sticky state. The add/subtract path carries those 53 retained bits plus overflow and rounding positions in a 57-bit active slice of the shared work register. This keeps the 80387 exponent range but provides binary64-class precision rather than the 80387's full 64-bit significand. Results produced by arithmetic therefore have reduced precision even when stored as m80. DSP-based multiplication. The two 53-bit significands are split into 27- and 26-bit limbs. Four 27-by-27 products map onto Cyclone V DSP blocks and are assembled into an exact 106-bit intermediate product. This avoids a large LUT multiplier while retaining all bits needed by the common rounder. With these measures, the FPU hierarchy uses about 5,100 ALMs in the 85 MHz release fit. The complete z486 PC build, including the FPU and peripherals, uses 35,686 of the DE10-Nano's 41,910 ALMs. Performance was optimized iteratively as well. In an early TurboQuake render-window profile, x87 instructions accounted for about 23% of retired instructions but 61% of instruction-attributed cycles. The numeric executor was active during only about 40% of those x87 cycles; command dispatch, operand transfer, stack access, launch, and retirement consumed the rest. Performance work therefore addressed both sides of the CPU/FPU boundary: faster conversion and arithmetic schedules, a direct m32 path for common memory operands, and shorter command sequencing. TurboQuake progress at major x87 milestones. The gains came from both arithmetic and CPU/coprocessor scheduling. The first complete x87 build ran TurboQuake at 2.7 FPS at 50 MHz. The current release reaches about 6.3 FPS at the 85 MHz board clock. Performance evaluation Dhrystone: CPU performance Dhrystone provides a compact measure of integer pipeline efficiency, largely separate from clock rate and whole-system behavior. The evaluation covers z386, ao486, z486, PicoRV32, and VexRiscv. The benchmark uses the conventional VAX 11/780 normalization: DMIPS/MHz = iterations * 1,000,000 / (cycles * 1757) All builds use -O3 -fno-inline, no link-time optimization, and no explicit register declarations. The x86 cores execute the same i386 binary produced by GCC 11.4. PicoRV32 and VexRiscv execute the same C source as RV32IM, built by GCC 10.2. Each harness returns memory data at the earliest cycle allowed by its interface. z386 and z486 retain the release 8 KB instruction and 8 KB data caches; ao486 retains its native cache organization. Core Cycles/iteration CPI DMIPS/MHz Cyclone V ALMs z386 2,526.4 4.101 0.225 15,545 ao486 2,934.0 4.556 0.194 15,190 z486 1,725.0 2.800 0.330 21,906 PicoRV32 2,336.1 4.172 0.244 1,202 VexRiscv 780.1 1.393 0.730 1,029 The ALM figures come from standalone seed-1 fits on the DE10-Nano Cyclone V, all using the same z486_MiSTer production settings. The configurations are not feature-equivalent: the two RISC-V cores omit caches, an MMU, segmentation, protected mode, legacy I/O and interrupts, and floating point. A z486 build without x87 uses 16,329 ALMs, only 5.0% more than z386. Locally reproduced Dhrystone 2.1 efficiency. Higher is better. x86 and RISC-V use different binaries, so the RISC-V results provide architectural context rather than an ISA-neutral ranking. z486 uses 31.7% fewer cycles per iteration than z386 and 41.2% fewer than ao486. Its DMIPS/MHz is 46% above z386 and 70% above ao486. At the tested MiSTer clocks, the results are 28.05 DMIPS for z486 at 85 MHz, 19.15 for z386 at 85 MHz, and 17.46 for ao486 at 90 MHz. Source repositories, release clocks, and upstream results are listed in Further information and references. Compiler and memory-interface choices have a large effect on Dhrystone scores. The local no-cache VexRiscv RV32IM build reaches 0.730 DMIPS/MHz, below the project's published 1.21 DMIPS/MHz for its full no-cache configuration and documented benchmark environment. PicoRV32 reaches 0.244 DMIPS/MHz locally; its project reports 0.516 with the look-ahead memory interface and 0.305 without it. The published configurations are linked in the final reference section. CPI is derived from each binary's retired instruction count, so it should be compared across ISAs less precisely than cycles per iteration or DMIPS/MHz. The ao486 retirement event also occurs at a different pipeline boundary from the z386 and z486 event. These differences do not affect the measured cycle counts. Doom: whole-system performance Doom measures whole-system performance rather than isolated integer pipeline efficiency. Its timedemo exercises instruction decode and execution, caches, external memory, and video writes. All measurements use the same MiSTer setup at each core's release clock: 85 MHz for z386 and z486, and 90 MHz for ao486. Board-measured DOS performance on the same MiSTer setup. Higher is better. At maximum detail, z486 reaches 29.1 FPS in the Doom timedemo, 39% faster than ao486's 21.0 FPS and 27% faster than z386 v0.4's 23.0 FPS. The independent 3DBench result shows the same ordering. Doom represents complete DOS-system behavior; Dhrystone more directly isolates integer pipeline efficiency. Verification Verification for a pipelining CPU is harder than a sequential one as there is more parallelism. A value may belong to the wrong instruction, a fault may cancel EX while leaving a younger commit active, or a cache operation may race with a store or DMA snoop. Validation therefore covers both instruction semantics and inter-stage ordering. The current validation stack includes: directed single-instruction tests; 9,410 real-mode and 1,220 protected-mode singlestep cases; protected-mode integration programs and the test386 suite; focused instruction/data cache race tests; x87 command, stack, executor, TestFloat, and CPU integration tests; differential x87 traces against QEMU and a retired reference executor; deterministic Doom and Quake snapshots with RAM hashes; full-system DOS, Windows 3.1, Doom, Quake, demos, and game simulations; and five-seed Quartus comparisons followed by physical MiSTer testing. ao486 is the closest related open-source design and the CPU behind the established ao486 MiSTer core. It implements a 486SX-class integer processor with broad software compatibility, but no integrated x87. ao486 implements the 486 architecture directly; z486 instead evolved from a microcoded 386 core, adding a pipelined frontend, generated hardwired recipes for common instructions, and an application-focused x87. Because both run the same PC software on the same FPGA platform, their whole-system Doom results are more informative than area alone. Open RISC-V cores cover a larger design space, from multi-cycle PicoRV32 to configurable pipelined VexRiscv. They provide useful Dhrystone and FPGA-efficiency reference points, but are not area-equivalent alternatives: the x86 cores also implement variable-length decode, segmented and paged protection, legacy execution modes, and a much larger compatibility surface. Potential work includes: improving sustained cache-hit load throughput; reclaiming more redundant instruction-boundary slots through measured, timing-safe chaining; completing the remaining 486 and x87 instructions; moving x87 arithmetic toward the full 64-bit significand of the 80387; improving 85 MHz timing margin while retaining current CPI and area; and continuing compatibility work driven by DOS and Windows games and applications. Conclusion z486 shows that a microcode-driven 386 foundation can be extended into a practical pipelined FPGA CPU without replacing its complex architectural behavior with a large behavioral instruction engine. The D1/D2 frontend and generated hardwired recipes give common instructions i486-like timing, while the original microcode continues to handle protection, faults, task switching, and other irregular operations. A compact integrated x87 extends that approach to the floating-point subset needed by Quake. The resulting core reaches 0.330 DMIPS/MHz and runs the maximum-detail Doom timedemo at 29.1 FPS on MiSTer, compared with 0.194 DMIPS/MHz and 21.0 FPS for ao486. It does so at 85 MHz in 35,686 of the DE10-Nano's 41,910 ALMs. The remaining two-cycle load latency, incomplete x87 instruction set, and limited timing margin also show where the FPGA implementation still differs from a complete i486-class processor. blocks.html_en: By the time the i486 was designed, x86 instructions already had a complex, variable-length encoding. Prefixes, two-byte opcodes, ModR/M and SIB bytes, displacements, and immediates are all optional, and some fields cannot be located until earlier fields have been interpreted. Earlier x86 frontends used sequential decode machinery that could take several clocks. The i486 instead divides decode into two explicit pipeline stages: D1 determines instruction structure and boundaries, while D2 captures literals and generates addresses.

blocks.html_en: The frontend uses a 32-byte prefetch queue filled one 16-byte instruction-cache line at a time. Like the i486 queue, it provides separate ports for structural and literal decode: a registered 64-bit D1 window and a 32-bit literal window. Prefixes and 0F consume extra structural cycles. An opcode and optional ModR/M normally complete in one D1 clock, while SIB parsing can use a retained sub-cycle. A one-entry registered skid buffer lets D1 run ahead when D2 is occupied without requiring a deep decoded-instruction queue.

blocks.html_en: The release MiSTer configuration has separate 8 KB instruction and 8 KB data caches, both four-way set associative with 16-byte lines. blocks.html_en: • Reduced internal precision. The architectural stack and transfer paths retain raw 80-bit temporary-real values, preserving untouched FLD m80 to FSTP m80 round trips and save/restore data. Arithmetic decodes an operand into a 15-bit exponent and a 53-bit significand, with separate guard, round, and sticky state. The add/subtract path carries those 53 retained bits plus overflow and rounding positions in a 57-bit active slice of the shared work register. This keeps the 80387 exponent range but provides binary64-class precision rather than the 80387's full 64-bit significand. Results produced by arithmetic therefore have reduced precision even when stored as m80.

blocks.html_en: z486 shows that a microcode-driven 386 foundation can be extended into a practical pipelined FPGA CPU without replacing its complex architectural behavior with a large behavioral instruction engine. The D1/D2 frontend and generated hardwired recipes give common instructions i486-like timing, while the original microcode continues to handle protection, faults, task switching, and other irregular operations. A compact integrated x87 extends that approach to the floating-point subset needed by Quake.

content_html_zh:
我在5月份发布了开源80386 CPU核心z386，并在6月份添加了80386提前启动优化。 早期启动将一条指令的地址生成与其前一条指令的完成重叠。 这是一个重要的 386 性能特性，但它也预览了更系统的 i486 管道。 MiSTer 核心需要更高的性能，因此我继续朝这个方向发展，并添加了更多 486 级机制。

结果是 z486，一个用 SystemVerilog 编写的开源、80486 级流水线 x86 CPU。 它将通用指令的硬连线、流水线执行与复杂架构行为的微代码相结合。

z486 不是 i486 克隆。 其设计借鉴了三个受 i486 启发的元素：

  1. 流水线 D1/D2 前端；
  2. 硬连线执行常见指令，并为复杂指令保留微代码；和
  3. 一个实验性集成 x87 单元，实现 Quake 所使用的子集。

在同一个 MiSTer 系统上，当前核心以 29.1 FPS 的最大细节运行 Doom timedemo，而 ao486 上的速度为 21.0 FPS。 对于测量的工作负载来说，这大约是 486DX2-66 级的性能。 Dhrystone 达到 0.330 DMIPS/MHz，而 z386 为 0.225，ao486 为 0.194。 这些结果表明，具有广泛架构支持（包括 x87）的实用流水线 x86 CPU 可以安装在中档 FPGA 上。

i486 五级流水线

有限状态或微编码 CPU 通过在单独的周期中执行解码、地址生成、内存访问、ALU 工作和提交来限制组合深度。 这支持高时钟频率，但为简单指令提供了高每指令周期 (CPI) 计数。 将所有工作合并到一个周期中可以降低 CPI，但会通过宽多路复用器和互连创建很长的路径。 流水线将寄存器的工作分开并重叠连续的指令。

可变长度 x86 指令需要与经典 RISC 流水线不同的级划分，通常写为 IF-ID-EX-MEM-WB。 i486 使用五个阶段：

Stage 主要工作
FI 将 16 字节行取出到指令队列中。
D1 解码前缀、操作码、ModR/M 结构、指令长度和 D2 操作。
D2 捕获位移或立即数据并计算有效地址。
EX 执行ALU或微码工作；访问高速缓存和 TLB 来获取内存指令。
WB 将 ALU 或加载结果写入寄存器文件。

两个解码阶段取代了单个 RISC ID 阶段，并且缓存访问发生在 EX 中，而不是在单独的 MEM 阶段中。 微编码指令可以使用多个 EX 周期。 因此，单时钟吞吐量是常见情况，而不是每条指令的属性。

英特尔的功能框图（与参考文献一起复制）显示了内部总线如何连接解码、地址生成、转换、缓存访问和执行。

解码可变长度 x86 指令

当 i486 被设计出来时，x86 指令已经有了复杂的、可变长度的编码。 前缀、两字节操​​作码、ModR/M 和 SIB 字节、位移和立即数都是可选的，并且某些字段在解释较早的字段之前无法定位。 早期的 x86 前端使用可能需要几个时钟的顺序解码机制。 相反，i486 将解码分为两个显式流水线阶段：D1 确定指令结构和边界，而 D2 捕获文字并生成地址。

在常见情况下，D1 一起解码操作码、ModR/M 和 SIB。 它还确定指令长度并告诉对齐器下一条指令和当前指令的文字的开始位置。 每个时钟处理一个字节的前缀，0F 转义消耗另一个 D1 时钟。

D2 每个时钟消耗一个 1 到 4 字节的位移或立即数。 同时，它读取基址寄存器和索引寄存器并计算有效地址。 预取队列中的独立结构端口和文字端口让 D1 处理一条指令，而 D2 处理其前一条指令。

常见表格在一小时内完成 D2。 两种情况扩展D2：

  • 同时具有位移和立即数的指令使用两个 D2 时钟；
  • 包含基址、位移和缩放索引的地址可以使用第二个 D2 时钟进行第二次加法。

这也是386早期想法的流水线版本。 在 386 上，指令队列在前一条指令的最后一个周期内呈现地址操作数。 在 i486 上，D2 是一个显式阶段，下一条指令执行相同的工作，而其前一条指令则占用 EX 和 WB。

额外的周期是经过深思熟虑的区域和时间权衡。 允许两个解码器从预取队列中每个可能的字节位置选择每个字段将需要大型对齐网络。 有界 D1 和 D2 窗口可快速保持常用指令，而不会使最坏情况对齐成为时钟关键数据路径的一部分。

加载、转发和指针加载延迟

当后继指令需要其前驱尚未写入寄存器文件的结果时，重叠指令会引入数据危险。 考虑紧接着 ALU 操作的加载：

mov eax, [esi]
add ebx, eax

当 ADD 到达 EX 时，加载结果位于 WB 中，但可能尚未通过正常的寄存器文件读取可见。 停止直到写入完成会造成数据加载延迟。

在 i486 上，给定缓存命中，转发使该值可用于同一周期中的普通相关 ALU 指令。 因此，i486 没有一般的数据加载延迟。

例外是使用加载的寄存器作为地址基址或索引的后继者：

mov eax, [esi]
mov ebx, [eax]

第二个MOV需要D2中的EAX来计算其内存访问将在EX中使用的有效地址。 这比 ALU 消费者需要该值早了一个阶段。 当第二条指令首先到达D2时，加载仍在EX中并且其结果不可用。 D2 必须停顿一个时钟，然后在负载前进到 WB 时接收值。 英特尔称其为指针加载延迟；如今，它通常被描述为地址生成互锁（AGI）。

消除这种延迟需要更早、更大的旁路网络。 相反，i486 接受指针依赖性的单周期气泡。

分支时序

i486 在推测性获取目标的同时评估 EX 中的条件分支。 未采用的 Jcc 会花费一个时钟，因为顺序管道已经存在。 执行的 Jcc、JMP 或近 CALL 从分支 EX 到目标 EX 需要三个时钟。

克劳福德报告说，英特尔评估了更积极的两周期采用分支设计，但它会使不采用分支变慢，并且需要更多的缓存机制。 公布的指令组合仅显示出约百分之一的总体优势。 实施的三周期采取、一周期不采取的政策更适合管道的其余部分。

z486 管道

以 i486 管道为指导，z486 保留了 FI、D1、D2 和 EX 阶段划分。 主要区别在于后端：普通整数结果在 EX 边缘提交，而不是通过通用 WB 阶段。

该实现将此阶段流程映射到共享相同地址、数据、内存、保护和浮点单元的硬连线和微编码控制路径。 RTL 也比 z386 更加模块化。 地址生成、整数执行、内存、硬连线控制和微排序被提取到单独的模块中，使 z486.sv 主要用作管道集成和跨单元粘合。 由此产生的顶级模块比 z386 短约三分之一：2.6K 行对 3.9K。

前端使用一个 32 字节预取队列，一次填充一个 16 字节指令高速缓存行。 与 i486 队列一样，它为结构解码和文字解码提供单独的端口：注册的 64 位 D1 窗口和 32 位文字窗口。 前缀和 0F 会消耗额外的结构周期。 操作码和可选的 ModR/M 通常在一个 D1 时钟内完成，而 SIB 解析可以使用保留的子周期。 当 D2 被占用时，单项注册滑动缓冲区可让 D1 提前运行，而不需要深度解码指令队列。

D1 解析微代码条目并将其启动到同步控制存储中。 因此，第一个控制字与解码指令及其文字一起在 D2 中可用。 D2 执行有效地址工作和危险检查； i_issue 是将完整的 D2 指令传输到 EX 的单个事件。

该组织将两个昂贵的操作排除在同一周期之外：

  • D2计算并重定位有效地址为线性地址；
  • 内存路径的下一部分对其进行转换并访问物理索引、物理标记的缓存。

发布的 MiSTer 配置具有独立的 8 KB 指令和 8 KB 数据缓存，两者都是与 16 字节线关联的四路集。 数据缓存通过三条目存储队列进行直写。 相反，i486 具有一个统一的 8 KB 缓存，并通过重叠虚拟索引和转换在一个时钟内完成缓存命中加载。 z486 的 L1 总容量是其两倍，但其更简单的物理索引、物理标记组织可序列化转换和缓存访问。 因此，最好情况下的整数加载需要两个时钟，而不是 i486 的一个。 让 VIPT 发挥作用是未来的工作。

回写组织

z486 与 i486 的不同之处在于后端。 普通 GPR、EIP、ESP、EFLAGS 和内部寄存器结果在 EX 时钟沿提交；没有通用的WB阶段。

这是 FPGA 特定的权衡。 通过完整的 WB 阶段保留依赖性时序需要广泛的旁路网络：较新的指令需要 EX 中待处理的 WB 值，并且对于地址依赖性，需要 D2 中较早的一个阶段。 在早期的实验中，额外的路由和操作数复用延迟的成本高于将提交移出所保存的 EX 关键路径的成本。 因此，z486 仅保留狭窄的、特定于操作的延迟状态，例如移位器结果或挂起的加载提交。

硬接线常用说明

流水线不会自动删除原始 386 微代码的简单操作的最小两个周期。 例如寄存器MOV是：

003  SRCREG                           PASS    RNI
004  SIGMA  -> DSTREG

第一个字通过 ALU 传递源并宣布运行下一条指令 (RNI)。 由于定序器具有架构延迟槽，因此第二个字仍然执行并写入结果。 尽管前端速度更快，但不变地运行此序列将保留两个周期的 EX 报废率。

i486 通过硬连线逻辑控制频繁指令，同时保留复杂情况的微代码。 z486 遵循相同的划分：硬连线和微编码控制都驱动共享整数数据路径。

食谱和 uSteps

生成脚本 script/ucode_optimize.py 生成 34 个硬连线指令配方的元数据。 每个配方包含一到三个活动 uStep。 uStep 将本机微码字与 D2 工作、架构提交、延迟时隙处理和危险的生成字段相结合。

对于 MOV r,r，优化后的字仍使用原始 PASS 数据路径，但生成的目标编码在同一边上提交 ALU 结果。 因此，硬连线配方在一个活动插槽中完成相同的工作。

链接

一旦延迟槽被证明是多余的，z486 就可以启动其中的下一个硬连线指令。 这称为链接。 它适用于单 uStep 配方和多 uStep 配方：一 uStep 配方可以启动其注册的后继者，而多 uStep 配方可以在接近其最终 RNI 字时启动队列头。 重复的一uStep链提供持续的每时钟一条指令执行。

在链接之前，控制单元检查：

  • 源、目标和字节寄存器重叠；
  • 标记生产者/消费者依赖关系；
  • 有效地址基址、索引和 ESP 依赖关系；
  • 待装载和转移目的地；
  • D2 和控制店驻留；
  • 内存或堆栈槽是否仍然包含实际工作；和
  • 故障、中断、陷阱、单步和 CPU 限制。

内存、堆栈和分支

配方不限于寄存器操作：

  • MOV r,[m] 准备 D2 中的地址并使用两 uStep 加载配方，保留实际结果槽；
  • 存储和 PUSH 保留其内存槽，因为接受和 ESP 更新是架构工作；
  • 安全未采取的 Jcc 可以折叠到前驱边界中；
  • Jcc 和 JMP 在一个有界分支 uStep 中使用 D2 计算的相对目标；和
  • close CALL 结合了重定向、发布的返回地址存储和 ESP 提交。

当前最佳情况的指令时序是：

辅导班 80386 i486 z486
MOV r,r / ADD r,r 2 1 1
MOV r,[m] 4 1 2
MOV [m],r 2 1 1
ADD r,[m] 5 2 3
JCC 未采取 3 1 1
JCC采取 about 9 3 3
JMP 已采取 about 9 3 3
近呼叫 about 9 3 4
XCHG [m], r 5 5 5

剩下的主要差距是内存延迟：z486 的 PIPT 数据缓存需要两个时钟才能加载命中。 时序安全的 VIPT 设计是实现 i486 单时钟负载的一种可能途径。

没有硬连线配方的指令继续通过通用微定序器。 因此，任务切换、调用门、特权转换、描述符更新、嵌套故障、异常前缀和其他复杂行为保留了原始微代码例程及其延迟时隙假设。

z486 包含一个实验性集成 x87 浮点单元。 它还不是一个完整的 x87 实现，但它实现了足够的指令集来运行 Quake 和 TurboQuake。 它的组织遵循原始 80387 的主要边界，其框图出现在参考文献中：命令和堆栈控制、微编码数字执行器、共享有效数算术以及用于超越函数的单独 CORDIC 引擎。

  • x87_bridge 将 80386 命令/数据端口协议转换为已注册的就绪/有效传输；
  • x87_control 拥有命令解码、堆栈、TOP、标签、状态、异常和架构提交；
  • x87_executor 在共享转换和算术资源上运行生成的 256 字水平控制存储；和
  • 合格的 direct-m32 覆盖从常见游戏指令中删除了长 386 命令/数据传输循环，同时保留正常的分页和故障检查。

仅整数的 z386 内核已经占用了大约 15,000 个 ALM，而带有缓存、内存控制和外设的完整 PC 配置则超过了 25,000 个。 DE10-Nano 上的 Cyclone V 提供 41,910 个 ALM，因此传统的 FPU 很容易耗尽剩余容量，或者使设计无法进行布局和布线。 三种实施选择使该装置保持在有限的区域预算内：

  1. 水平微代码和共享算术。 同步 256 字 x 64 位控制存储对数字执行器进行排序。 每个水平字独立地控制流程、操作数准备、分类、加/减和移位路线、迭代引擎、舍入状态、结果打包、提交和 CORDIC 暂存访问。 这取代了大型解码操作选择器，直接控制每个步骤更新的状态。 加法、归一化、转换和舍入共享 68 位工作寄存器和加法器。 除法和平方根重用迭代数据路径，而不常见的先验指令则使用微编码、面向肢体的 CORDIC 引擎。
  2. 内部精度降低。 架构堆栈和传输路径保留原始 80 位临时实数值，保留未受影响的 FLD m80 到 FSTP m80 往返以及保存/恢复数据。 算术将操作数解码为 15 位指数和 53 位有效数，并具有单独的保护、舍入和粘性状态。 加/减路径携带共享工作寄存器的 57 位活动片中的这 53 个保留位以及溢出和舍入位置。 这保留了 80387 的指数范围，但提供了二进制 64 级精度，而不是 80387 的完整 64 位有效数。 因此，即使存储为 m80，算术产生的结果也会降低精度。
  3. 基于 DSP 的乘法。 两个 53 位有效数被分为 27 位和 26 位部分。 四个 27×27 产品映射到 Cyclone V DSP 模块，并组装成精确的 106 位中间产品。 这避免了大的 LUT 乘法器，同时保留了公共舍入器所需的所有位。

通过这些措施，FPU 层次结构在 85 MHz 版本中使用了大约 5,100 个 ALM。 完整的 z486 PC 构建（包括 FPU 和外设）使用 DE10-Nano 的 41,910 个 ALM 中的 35,686 个。

性能也经过迭代优化。 在早期的 TurboQuake 渲染窗口配置文件中，x87 指令约占退役指令的 23%，但占指令归因周期的 61%。 数字执行器仅在大约 40% 的 x87 周期中处于活动状态；命令调度、操作数传输、堆栈访问、启动和退出消耗了其余部分。 因此，性能工作涉及 CPU/FPU 边界的两侧：更快的转换和算术调度、公共内存操作数的直接 m32 路径以及更短的命令排序。

第一个完整的 x87 版本在 50 MHz 下以 2.7 FPS 运行 TurboQuake。 当前版本在 85 MHz 板时钟下达到约 6.3 FPS。

绩效评估

Dhrystone：CPU 性能

Dhrystone 提供了一种紧凑的整数管道效率测量方法，很大程度上独立于时钟速率和整个系统行为。 评估涵盖 z386、ao486、z486、PicoRV32 和 VexRiscv。

该基准测试使用传统的 VAX 11/780 标准化：

DMIPS/MHz = iterations * 1,000,000 / (cycles * 1757)

所有构建都使用 -O3 -fno-inline，没有链接时优化，也没有显式的寄存器声明。 x86 内核执行 GCC 11.4 生成的相同 i386 二进制文件。 PicoRV32 和 VexRiscv 执行与 RV32IM 相同的 C 源代码，由 GCC 10.2 构建。 每个线束在其接口允许的最早周期返回内存数据。 z386和z486保留释放8KB指令和8KB数据缓存； ao486 保留其本机缓存组织。

Core 周期/迭代 CPI DMIPS/MHz Cyclone V ALM
z386 2,526.4 4.101 0.225 15,545
ao486 2,934.0 4.556 0.194 15,190
z486 1,725.0 2.800 0.330 21,906
皮克RV32 2,336.1 4.172 0.244 1,202
威克斯瑞西克夫 780.1 1.393 0.730 1,029

ALM 数据来自 DE10-Nano Cyclone V 上的独立 Seed-1 拟合，全部使用相同的 z486_MiSTer 生产设置。 这些配置在功能上并不等效：两个 RISC-V 内核省略了缓存、MMU、分段、保护模式、传统 I/O 和中断以及浮点。 不带 x87 的 z486 版本使用 16,329 个 ALM，仅比 z386 多 5.0%。

z486 每次迭代使用的周期比 z386 少 31.7%，比 ao486 少 41.2%。 其DMIPS/MHz比z386高46%，比ao486高70%。 在测试的 MiSTer 时钟下，z486 在 85 MHz 时的结果为 28.05 DMIPS，z386 在 85 MHz 时的结果为 19.15，ao486 在 90 MHz 时的结果为 17.46。 更多信息和参考中列出了源存储库、发布时钟和上游结果。

编译器和内存接口的选择对 Dhrystone 分数有很大影响。 本地无缓存 VexRiscv RV32IM 构建达到 0.730 DMIPS/MHz，低于该项目为其完整无缓存配置和记录的基准环境发布的 1.21 DMIPS/MHz。 PicoRV32 本地达到 0.244 DMIPS/MHz；其项目报告使用前瞻内存接口时为 0.516，不使用前瞻内存接口时为 0.305。 已发布的配置在最终参考部分中有链接。

CPI 源自每个二进制文件的退役指令计数，因此跨 ISA 进行比较的精确度应该低于每次迭代周期或 DMIPS/MHz。 ao486 停用事件还发生在与 z386 和 z486 事件不同的管道边界处。 这些差异不会影响测量的循环计数。

Doom：整个系统性能

Doom 衡量的是整个系统的性能，而不是孤立的整数管道效率。 它的 timedemo 练习了指令解码和执行、缓存、外部存储器和视频写入。 所有测量均在每个内核的发布时钟上使用相同的 MiSTer 设置：z386 和 z486 为 85 MHz，ao486 为 90 MHz。

在最大细节下，z486 在《Doom time》演示中达到 29.1 FPS，比 ao486 的 21.0 FPS 快 39%，比 z386 v0.4 的 23.0 FPS 快 27%。 独立的 3DBench 结果显示了相同的顺序。 Doom 代表完整的 DOS 系统行为； Dhrystone 更直接地隔离整数管道效率。

确认

流水线 CPU 的验证比顺序 CPU 更难，因为并行性更高。 值可能属于错误的指令，故障可能会取消 EX，同时使较新的提交保持活动状态，或者缓存操作可能会与存储或 DMA 监听竞争。 因此，验证涵盖指令语义和阶段间排序。

当前的验证堆栈包括：

  • 定向单指令测试；
  • 9,410 个实模式和 1,220 个保护模式单步情况；
  • 保护模式集成程序和 test386 套件；
  • 重点指令/数据缓存竞争测试；
  • x87 命令、堆栈、执行器、TestFloat 和 CPU 集成测试；
  • 针对 QEMU 和已退役的参考执行器的差分 x87 跟踪；
  • 具有 RAM 哈希值的确定性 Doom 和 Quake 快照；
  • 全系统DOS、Windows 3.1、Doom、Quake、演示和游戏模拟；和
  • 五种子 Quartus 比较，然后进行物理 MiSTer 测试。

ao486 是最相关的开源设计，也是已建立的 ao486 MiSTer 核心背后的 CPU。 它实现了具有广泛软件兼容性的 486SX 级整数处理器，但没有集成 x87。 ao486直接实现486架构； z486 相反，是从微编码 386 核心演变而来，添加了流水线前端、为常用指令生成硬连线配方以及以应用程序为中心的 x87。 由于两者在相同的 FPGA 平台上运行相同的 PC 软件，因此它们的整个系统 Doom 结果比单独的区域提供更多信息。

开放 RISC-V 内核涵盖了更大的设计空间，从多周期 PicoRV32 到可配置流水线 VexRiscv。 它们提供了有用的 Dhrystone 和 FPGA 效率参考点，但不是面积等效的替代方案：x86 内核还实现了可变长度解码、分段和分页保护、传统执行模式以及更大的兼容性表面。

潜在的工作包括：

  • 提高持续缓存命中负载吞吐量；
  • 通过测量的、时序安全的链接回收更多冗余指令边界槽；
  • 完成剩余的 486 和 x87 指令；
  • 将 x87 算术移向 80387 的完整 64 位有效数；
  • 提高 85 MHz 时序余量，同时保留当前 CPI 和面积；和
  • 继续由 DOS 和 Windows 游戏和应用程序驱动的兼容性工作。

结论

z486 表明，微代码驱动的 386 基础可以扩展到实用的流水线 FPGA CPU，而无需用大型行为指令引擎替换其复杂的架构行为。 D1/D2 前端和生成的硬连线配方提供类似 i486 的通用指令计时，而原始微代码继续处理保护、故障、任务切换和其他不规则操作。 紧凑的集成 x87 将该方法扩展到 Quake 所需的浮点子集。

最终的核心达到 0.330 DMIPS/MHz，并在 MiSTer 上以 29.1 FPS 运行最大细节 Doom time 演示，而 ao486 的运行速度为 0.194 DMIPS/MHz 和 21.0 FPS。 它在 DE10-Nano 的 41,910 个 ALM 中的 35,686 个中以 85 MHz 执行此操作。 剩余的两个周期加载延迟、不完整的 x87 指令集和有限的时序余量也表明 FPGA 实现与完整的 i486 级处理器仍然不同。
